full_query: A 36-year-old G3P2002 woman presents to her obstetrician’s office for her 1st prenatal visit at 10 weeks and 2 days gestation. She has felt nauseous the last several mornings and has been tired for a few weeks. The patient has had 2 uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal deliveries at full term with her last child born 6 years ago. She is concerned about the risk of Down syndrome in this fetus, as her sister gave birth to an affected child at age 43. She has a history of generalized anxiety disorder, atopic dermatitis, and she is currently on escitalopram. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), pulse is 70/min, blood pressure is 121/67 mmHg, and respirations are 13/min. The patient appears anxious, but overall comfortable, and cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are unremarkable. Pelvic exam reveals normal external genitalia, a closed and soft cervix, a 10-week-sized uterus, and no adnexal masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for definitively determining whether this patient’s fetus has Down syndrome? (A) Amniocentesis (B) Anatomy ultrasound (C) Chorionic villus sampling (D) Genetic testing of patient’s sister (E) Nuchal translucency test

Identifying the Options for Definitive Diagnosis of Down Syndrome
Option A: Amniocentesis – Typically performed between 15 and 20 weeks' gestation
Option B: Anatomy ultrasound – Used for anatomical survey and detecting structural anomalies, usually performed around 18-20 weeks' gestation
Option C: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) – Can be performed between 10 and 13 weeks' gestation, making it suitable for early diagnosis
Option D: Genetic testing of patient’s sister – This would not directly inform the status of the current pregnancy
Option E: Nuchal translucency test – Performed between 11 and 14 weeks, useful as a screening test but not definitive
For definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome, invasive testing methods such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling are required
Given the patient’s current gestational age (10 weeks and 2 days), CVS is appropriate as it can be performed starting from 10 weeks
Amniocentesis is typically performed later in the pregnancy and would not be suitable at this stage
An anatomy ultrasound is not a definitive test for Down syndrome
Genetic testing of the sister is irrelevant to the diagnosis of the current fetus
Nuchal translucency is a screening test and not definitive
Considering the patient's gestational age and the need for a definitive diagnosis, the most appropriate next step is Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)
